Juan Chen: Bridging Data, Product Marketing, and Four Languages

How a technical foundation and global perspective shape modern product marketing at SAP.

📍 São Paulo, Brazil 🏢 SAP 📅 June 23, 2026
JC

Juan Chen

Director, Product Marketing — Data & Analytics · SAP

Digital transformation enthusiast. Technical background meets market storytelling. Building bridges between what data can do and what customers need to hear.

Product marketing has always lived at the intersection of technical capability and market narrative—the job is fundamentally about translation, taking what engineers build and turning it into something that resonates with the people who might buy it. Juan Chen operates at that intersection with an unusual advantage: he came up through the technical side before crossing over to marketing, and he does it across four languages in one of the world's most complex enterprise markets.

Based in São Paulo, Juan leads product marketing for SAP's Data & Analytics portfolio in Latin America—a region where digital transformation initiatives compete with infrastructure constraints, where enterprise software decisions often involve stakeholders across multiple countries and languages, and where the gap between what global headquarters produces and what local markets need can feel impossibly wide. Bridging that gap is the job.

The Technical Foundation

What makes Juan's approach distinctive is the depth of his technical foundation. He holds certifications in SAP Business Technology Platform and SAP Datasphere—not the kind of credentials you typically see on a marketing leader's profile, but exactly the kind of knowledge that changes how you talk about data products. When you've actually worked with the platform architecture, the positioning conversations sound different. You know which capabilities matter and which ones are marketing fiction.

"A digital transformation enthusiast with a strong technical background, who believes that technology should serve business outcomes—not the other way around."

That belief—technology serving business outcomes rather than the reverse—runs through how Juan approaches product marketing. The Pragmatic Institute certification (PMC Level I) reflects a structured approach to understanding market problems before jumping to product solutions, a discipline that's easy to talk about and hard to maintain when quarterly targets are pressing.

Four Languages, One Message

Juan operates fluently in Portuguese, Spanish, Chinese, and English—a combination that's rare even in global enterprise software. The practical implication: he can work directly with customers across Latin America without the translation layer that often strips nuance from market conversations, while also maintaining direct relationships with SAP's global teams and the increasingly important Asia-Pacific ecosystem.

In the Future of PMM curriculum, we talk about how AI is collapsing the distance between global content and local markets—translation becoming instant, localization becoming automated. But the human judgment about what resonates in São Paulo versus Mexico City versus Miami still requires someone who understands the cultural context, the business environment, the way decisions actually get made in each market. That's the layer that doesn't automate away.

Why This Matters Now

The data and analytics space is one of the most competitive in enterprise software—everyone from hyperscalers to startups is fighting for positioning around AI, data platforms, and the infrastructure layer that feeds machine learning models. The product marketers who succeed in this space tend to be the ones who can credibly discuss architecture with technical audiences while also crafting narratives that resonate in boardrooms. Juan represents that hybrid profile: technical enough to be credible, strategic enough to drive positioning, and multilingual enough to work across the fragmented markets where SAP competes.

As the AI transformation reshapes what product marketing looks like—and as we explore those changes through this curriculum—profiles like Juan's offer a glimpse of what the role requires in practice: technical depth, market intuition, and the ability to operate across boundaries that used to define separate jobs.
